slides.title: Announcements
items: Mid-course survey — group work and pacing.
A quick note on malloc() in embedded code.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 3 min. The malloc aside is ES 20 continuity, not ADC content — keep it short: embedded code allocates statically; a heap you cannot inspect on a part with 12 KB of RAM is a liability.

How the converter actually finds the answer

slides.title: What the Number Means
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 5 min. The reading already did this arithmetic — this is retrieval, not teaching. Compress to 3 if the room is quick; this is your first cut.

slides.title: Debrief
slides.body: 1.65 V is 2048 counts — not 2047. One count is worth about 0.81 mV.
slides.presenterNote: The 4095-vs-4096 argument is worth 60 seconds, not 3 minutes.

slides.title: Which Pins Can Do Analog?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 9 min. Budget 2–3 min just to get 30 people onto the right page of the right PDF. Datasheet Table 12 — the day's datasheet moment.

slides.title: CHSELR — bit n selects channel n
Debrief
slides.body: The header label, the port pin, and the ADC channel are three independent naming schemes. They agree for A0. They usually do not.
slides.presenterNote: This single sentence is what makes tonight's homework and Lab 4 Deliverable 1 possible. Do not skip it.

slides.title: The Test Circuit
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 10 min — only because the pots are pre-seated. If they were not, this part is 20+ for the slow tail.

slides.title: Debrief
slides.body: A potentiometer is a voltage divider you turn. The wiper is a source of voltage, not a control signal.

slides.title: The Four Registers
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 6 min. One register, one write, one thing to notice. All the examples use PA4 / channel 4 — theirs is PA0 / channel 0, so filling the blanks is transfer, not transcription.

slides.title: Waiting for a flag — you know this one
Writing ADCpot.c
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 20 min. THE CRUCIAL STEP — never cut this. Leave the diagnostic slide up for the whole part, and hand out the half-sheet version.

slides.title: Make the knob move the number
Finished early?
slides.body: Turn the knob to each mechanical end stop. Do you read exactly 0 and exactly 4095? If not — is the explanation in the potentiometer, or in the converter?
slides.presenterNote: The 2-minute stretch. The two big stretches are homework — say so, don't start them in class.

slides.title: Wait — How Did That Clear the Bit?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 7 min. The day's set-piece. If you must cut, cut it WHOLE — never truncate it. An unanswered puzzle is worse than one never raised.

slides.title: Debrief
slides.body: On a status register, writing 1 clears and writing 0 does nothing — so a plain assignment is safe and &= ~mask is not.
slides.presenterNote: Stay on the status-register case. Do NOT talk about interrupts landing mid-sequence or atomic set/clear — interrupts arrive Day 8, and that argument is BSRR's motivation in the timers chapter.

slides.title: Successive Approximation, Live
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 4 min, compressible to 2 as a whole-class call-and-response. Block diagram and timing are in the book's Reference section — do not re-teach them here; the reading already has them.

slides.title: Today, and where it goes
items: A count is a number of steps: V = count × 3.3 / 4096.
The datasheet says which pins do analog, and on which channel.
Configure once; then start, wait, read — every sample.
Status registers clear by writing 1, because two parties write them.
One comparison per bit is why a conversion takes ~14 clocks.
Lab 4 starts exactly where tonight's homework ends.
